before.content_html:
Migration Is the Long British Story

Britain has been shaped by people arriving from elsewhere for at least twelve hundred years. Vikings, Normans, medieval Jewish communities, Flemish weavers, Huguenots, Irish famine migrants, Eastern European Jewish refugees, Caribbean Windrush passengers and Ugandan Asians are all part of the same long thread. The historian David Olusoga has argued that Britain’s story cannot be told without these arrivals: hostility and welcome have run alongside each other in every period. The thematic study you are about to begin asks you to track that story across four periods — medieval, early modern, eighteenth and nineteenth century, and modern Britain — and to spot what changed, what stayed the same, and which factors drove each shift.

Key Fact

The thematic study covers four periods: c800–c1500 (medieval), c1500–c1700 (early modern), c1700–c1900 (industrial), and c1900–present (modern). Examiners reward answers that move between periods within a single paragraph rather than treating migration as a 20th-century story only.

The Four Key Factors

The Edexcel specification names four key factors that drive change in migration: institutions (government and Church), religion, economic influences, and attitudes in society. Most exam questions are really asking which of these mattered most at a given moment. The 1290 expulsion of England’s Jewish population, for example, mixes institutions (a royal decree from Edward I) with religion (Christian hostility) and economics (royal debts owed to Jewish lenders). The 1948 British Nationality Act mixes institutions (Parliament) with end-of-Empire politics and post-war labour shortages. Strong answers name the factor explicitly.

Alongside the four factors, historians use push and pull factors to explain why people moved at all. Push factors drove people away from home — famine in Ireland in the 1840s, pogroms in the Russian Empire from 1881, the expulsion of Asians from Uganda in 1972. Pull factors drew them to Britain — jobs in the cloth industry, royal protection for moneylenders, post-war NHS recruitment, the legal right to enter under the 1948 Nationality Act. Edexcel guidance is clear: focus mainly on what pulled people TO Britain, but show some awareness of what pushed them away from home.

Many students treat the Empire Windrush in 1948 as the start of British migration history, and treat earlier arrivals as ‘invasions’. The thematic study explicitly demands twelve centuries of continuous migration. The historian Miranda Kaufmann has documented over sixty parish baptisms of Africans in Tudor England between 1500 and 1640; Hanseatic merchants ran a trading enclave in London from the medieval period; Huguenots reshaped Spitalfields silk weaving after 1685. Top-band thematic essays move between at least two of the four periods within a single paragraph. Restricting yourself to the post-1948 story will cap your mark.

Change, Continuity and Turning Points

The thematic study is not a list of arrivals; it is a study of second-order concepts — the analytical ideas historians use to make sense of the past. The most important here are change (how migration patterns altered between periods), continuity (what stayed the same — the legal idea of the ‘alien’, religious refugee waves, hostility from press and politicians), and turning points (the 1290 expulsion, the 1685 Huguenot wave, the 1905 Aliens Act, the 1948 British Nationality Act, the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act). Knowing your turning points by date is what lets you write across periods quickly under exam pressure.

It is a mistake to assume there is a fixed group of ‘indigenous Britons’ against which everyone else is foreign. Each successive wave — Anglo-Saxons, Vikings, Normans, Huguenots, Irish, Jewish, Caribbean — was at first treated as ‘foreign’ and was later folded into the idea of ‘British’. Britishness is a constructed identity, not a biological one. This is why historians like Robert Winder describe migration as the engine of British history rather than its disruption.

Sources and the Notting Hill Site

The Edexcel paper splits into a thematic study (worth 36 marks) and a historic environment (worth 16 marks). For Notting Hill, c1948–c1970, you will work with both local sources — for example the West Indian Gazette, council and Metropolitan Police records, oral memoirs — and national sources like Times and Guardian coverage, government immigration files, census data and Pathé reports. The 8-mark source-utility question asks you to weigh up content, provenance and your own knowledge together; saying ‘it’s biased so it’s not useful’ is explicitly capped by examiners.

Edexcel question stems are signposted. ‘Describe two features’ (4 marks) wants two precise features with one developed detail each — not a paragraph of context. ‘Explain why’ (8 marks) wants at least two reasons developed with specific period detail. ‘Make and defend a judgement’ (16 marks) wants a clear, signposted judgement supported across at least two periods, using both stimulus points AND a self-generated factor. The 12-mark historic environment essay wants explicit links between Notting Hill specifics (a named street, a named individual) and wider context (housing shortage, colour bar, end of Empire). Spotting which factor — institutions, religion, economy, attitudes — the question is steering you towards is the single most valuable skill in the unit.

Key Fact

The four key factors that drive change in migration are institutions, religion, economic influences and attitudes in society. Almost every exam question is steered towards one or two of these — naming the factor explicitly is what unlocks the higher mark band.

SPaG marks reward consistent use of period-specific terminology (Danelaw, Huguenot, Aliens Act, Commonwealth) so weave these in throughout.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the four key factors used to explain migration in this period.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two valid features):
• Institutions — government and Church decisions (e.g. royal decrees such as Edward I's 1290 expulsion of Jews; Acts of Parliament such as the 1948 British Nationality Act) shape who can come and stay.
• Religion — religious persecution abroad (e.g. the 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes pushing Huguenots to Britain) and religious tolerance or hostility at home shape migration patterns.
• Economic influences — labour demand (e.g. cloth weaving in 16th-century Sandwich, post-war NHS recruitment in the 1950s) and trade networks pull migrants in.
• Attitudes in society — hostility (e.g. the British Brothers' League before 1905) or welcome (e.g. parish charity for Huguenots) shapes the migrant experience.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to causes of migration without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why historians study migration to Britain across the long period from c800 to the present, rather than starting with the Empire Windrush in 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail from the period.

Indicative content:
• Each successive wave (Vikings, Normans, Jewish communities, Huguenots, Irish, Jewish East Enders, Caribbean) shaped British institutions, language and economy in lasting ways — starting in 1948 erases that long influence.
• The legal idea of the ‘alien’ runs from medieval Hanseatic merchants through the 1905 Aliens Act — only a long view shows that continuity.
• Black presence in Britain predates Windrush by centuries: Miranda Kaufmann documented over sixty parish baptisms of Africans in Tudor England (1500–1640).
• Patterns of religious refugee migration (Huguenots after 1685, Jewish refugees after 1881, Ugandan Asians in 1972) only become visible when the four periods are studied together.
• Examiners explicitly reward thematic answers that move between at least two periods within a paragraph; restricting to the post-1948 story is capped.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons, each developed with specific period detail and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail; links to the question are present but less developed.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of one wave of migration without explaining why the long view matters.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of push and pull factors in migration to Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Push factors are reasons people leave their country of origin (e.g. the Great Famine in Ireland 1845–52; pogroms in the Russian Empire from 1881; the expulsion of Ugandan Asians in 1972).
• Pull factors are reasons migrants choose a particular destination (e.g. royal protection for medieval Jewish moneylenders, post-war NHS recruitment, the legal right to enter under the 1948 Nationality Act).
• Edexcel guidance focuses mainly on pull factors to Britain, with some awareness of push factors abroad.
• Push and pull often work together — Huguenots were pushed by Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 and pulled by the silk-weaving economy in Spitalfields.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to migration without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting economic influences as the most important factor:
• The cloth industry pulled Flemish and Walloon weavers to Sandwich and Canterbury in the 16th century, and Huguenot silk weavers to Spitalfields after 1685.
• Post-war Britain faced severe labour shortages from 1945; the NHS, London Transport and the textile industry actively recruited Caribbean and South Asian workers.
• Trade networks drew Hanseatic merchants to the medieval Steelyard and supported Jewish royal financiers like Aaron of Lincoln.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors):
• Institutions were decisive at turning points: Edward I's 1290 expulsion, the 1905 Aliens Act, the 1948 British Nationality Act, the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act — each Act reshaped who could come and stay.
• Religion drove major waves: the 1561 stranger churches at Sandwich; the 1685 Huguenot wave following the revocation of the Edict of Nantes; Eastern European Jewish refugees after the 1881 pogroms.
• Attitudes in society shaped reception independently of economics: anti-Catholic hostility to Irish migrants in the 1850s; the 1958 Notting Hill attacks during a period of full employment.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across at least two periods, uses accurate period vocabulary, includes a self-generated factor alongside the stimulus, and reaches a clear, signposted judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (e.g. push factor, pull factor, Huguenot, Aliens Act, Commonwealth, alien).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how the ‘alien’ legal status worked in British history.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• ‘Alien’ was the medieval and early modern legal category for people not born under the English crown — for example Hanseatic merchants in London or Flemish weavers in Sandwich.
• Aliens often paid higher taxes (e.g. medieval ‘tallage’ on Jewish communities) and faced restrictions on landownership and trade.
• The Aliens Act of 1905 was the first peacetime British immigration control, designed specifically to restrict poor Eastern European Jewish refugees.
• The status persisted in different forms: by 1948 the British Nationality Act created a common Commonwealth citizenship, but later Acts (1962, 1968) reintroduced restrictions.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to migration laws without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ‘turning points’ matter to a thematic study of migration in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Turning points mark moments when policy or attitude shifted decisively (e.g. the 1290 expulsion of Jews, the 1905 Aliens Act, the 1948 British Nationality Act, the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act) — they let students structure long-period answers.
• They make change visible against continuity — the 1948 Act looks like dramatic change, but it sits alongside the continued legal idea of the ‘alien’ that runs from medieval England.
• They allow comparison across periods — the 1685 Huguenot wave (religious refugee, welcomed) compared with the 1881–82 Jewish East End wave (religious refugee, met with the 1905 Aliens Act).
• Examiners reward judgements anchored to specific dates and Acts; vague references to ‘changes over time’ without named turning points are capped.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific dated turning points and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of one Act without explaining why turning points matter.

lessons.title: Vikings, Anglo-Saxons and the Danelaw, c800–c1066

before.content_html:
From Raid to Settlement

Britain’s first wave of recorded large-scale migration in the period c800–c1066 came from Scandinavia. The earliest Viking raids on Lindisfarne in 793 are famous, but the decisive shift was the arrival of the Heathen Army in 865. Within a decade this force had taken Northumbria, East Anglia and much of Mercia. The pull factors were clear: Britain offered fertile land, weak political resistance after years of internal Anglo-Saxon warfare, and a coastline studded with rich monasteries. The push factors included population pressure in Scandinavia and the political fragmentation of Norse societies. By the 870s, large numbers of Danish and Norwegian families were arriving not as raiders but as settlers.

Key Fact

Vikings did not arrive only as raiders. After the Heathen Army landed in 865, large numbers came as settlers and farmers, and by the 870s entire Scandinavian families were establishing themselves in eastern and northern England.

The Treaty of Wedmore and the Danelaw

In 878, after defeating the Viking leader Guthrum at the Battle of Edington, Alfred the Great agreed the Treaty of Wedmore. Guthrum was baptised as a Christian and accepted a boundary running roughly along the Roman road of Watling Street, from London to Chester. North and east of that line, Scandinavian law and custom would prevail. This area became known as the Danelaw. It was not a separate Viking kingdom but a recognised zone of Norse settlement and legal custom inside England.

Within the Danelaw, the unit of local government was the wapentake — the equivalent of the Anglo-Saxon hundred elsewhere in England. Disputes were settled at wapentake meetings rather than at hundred courts. Place names still mark the difference: villages ending in -by (Whitby, Grimsby, Selby) and -thorpe (Scunthorpe, Mablethorpe) were Norse settlements; place names ending in -tun were Anglo-Saxon. Roughly 1,500 modern English place names in the Danelaw counties are Scandinavian in origin.

Many students describe Vikings only through Lindisfarne and longships. The thematic study expects you to track the move from raid to permanent settlement. After 865, Viking newcomers cleared land, married into Anglo-Saxon families, paid taxes, attended local courts and converted to Christianity (Guthrum did so as part of the Treaty of Wedmore). The Danelaw was a place of farming villages, market towns and trade, not a series of beach raids. Treating Vikings as ‘just raiders’ misses the migration story the spec is asking about.

Anglo-Saxons as Earlier Migrants

It is also a mistake to treat Anglo-Saxons as the original ‘native’ population against whom Vikings were foreign. The Anglo-Saxons were themselves migrants — descendants of Angles, Saxons and Jutes who arrived from northern Germany and Denmark in the fifth and sixth centuries. By the 800s they were ‘British’ in identity, but only a few centuries earlier their ancestors had also been arrivals. This is exactly the pattern you saw in lesson one: each wave of newcomers was treated as ‘foreign’ at first and folded into ‘British’ later. Both Anglo-Saxons and Vikings spoke languages from the same Germanic family, which is why Old English and Old Norse mingled rather than clashed.

Cnut and the Anglo-Scandinavian Crown

Viking influence reached its political peak in 1016 when Cnut became king of England, ruling an empire that also included Denmark and Norway. Cnut governed England by working with Anglo-Saxon institutions: he kept the existing system of shires and ealdormen, issued law codes that drew on earlier Anglo-Saxon traditions, and gave generously to English monasteries. By the time of his death in 1035, Anglo-Scandinavian England had a stable shared culture. The institutions key factor (royal government and Church) had absorbed the migrants rather than been overturned by them.

The lasting impact of Viking migration runs deep. In language, hundreds of common English words are Norse in origin: sky, law, egg, knife, they, them and their. In law, the wapentake survived in northern England into the Middle Ages, and aspects of trial by jury developed from Scandinavian custom. In economy, Viking trade networks linked York and Lincoln to Dublin, Bergen and the Black Sea — bringing silver, slaves, amber and ironwork through English ports. None of this would have happened if migration had stopped at the raid stage.

Key Fact

Viking migration left lasting marks on language (around 1,500 Scandinavian place names; everyday words like sky, law, they), on law (the Danelaw, the wapentake, early forms of trial by jury) and on the economy (trade networks linking York and Lincoln to Dublin, Bergen and beyond).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Danelaw was established in England in 878.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail from the period.

Indicative content:
• Military stalemate — Alfred the Great defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878 but lacked the resources to drive Scandinavian settlers out of the north and east, so a negotiated boundary made political sense.
• Religious factor — the Treaty of Wedmore required Guthrum's baptism, which gave Alfred a Christian peace partner inside the Church and reduced future raiding.
• Economic factor — large numbers of Scandinavian families had already cleared and farmed land in eastern England since 865; expulsion would have wrecked the local economy.
• Institutional factor — recognising the Danelaw allowed Anglo-Saxon law to operate in Wessex while Norse legal custom continued in the north, stabilising both regions.
• Cultural compatibility — Old English and Old Norse came from the same Germanic family, which made coexistence and intermarriage easier than expulsion.

lessons.title: Case Study: York under the Vikings

before.content_html:
From Eboracum to Jorvik

When the Heathen Army captured York in 866, the city was already centuries old. The Romans had founded Eboracum as a legionary fortress in 71 CE; under the Anglo-Saxons it became Eoforwic, a centre of Northumbrian kingship and Christian learning. The Vikings did not create York from nothing. What they did was rename it Jorvik, expand it dramatically, and turn it into one of the largest trading towns in northern Europe. Studying York is the spec’s case study for the medieval period — a chance to see the four key factors (institutions, religion, economic influences, attitudes) all working at once on a single named place.

Key Fact

York was Roman Eboracum, then Anglo-Saxon Eoforwic, before becoming Viking Jorvik after 866. Vikings inherited and expanded an existing city; they did not invent it.

A Capital City and a Royal Court

From 866 Jorvik became the capital of the Viking kingdom of York — a real political institution with its own kings, coinage and courts. The most famous king was Eric Bloodaxe, who reigned from 947–948 and again from 952–954. His expulsion and death at Stainmore in 954 ended independent Viking kingship in England, but Norse culture and population remained dominant in the city for generations. Jorvik issued silver pennies stamped with the names of its kings, including Cnut and the Anglo-Scandinavian moneyer Hildulf — physical evidence that institutions of government were running smoothly in the hands of Viking-descended rulers.

Coppergate and the Archaeology of Daily Life

Most of what we know about ordinary life in Jorvik comes from the Coppergate excavation, carried out by the York Archaeological Trust between 1976 and 1981. Waterlogged conditions had preserved timber buildings, leather shoes, textiles, hair combs and even fragments of food in extraordinary detail. The street name itself comes from Old Norse kopari-gata — ‘the street of the cup-makers’. Coppergate showed Jorvik as a working town of densely packed wooden houses, narrow alleys, workshops, latrines and back yards full of crafts.

Excavated workshops produced amber jewellery, glass beads, leather shoes, ironwork and bone combs — the everyday output of the Coppergate craftsmen. Coin hoards and Arabic dirhams found in the city show York’s reach into a wider trading world. The economic factor pull is overwhelming here: Jorvik was a magnet because work and wealth were available.

A frequent error is to treat Vikings as the founders of York. They were not. Roman Eboracum had been a legionary capital for centuries, and Anglo-Saxon Eoforwic was already an important Northumbrian centre with an archbishop and a school of learning. The Viking transformation came in scale and character: street layout was reshaped, the population grew rapidly, and the city was wired into a North Sea trading network. Strong answers credit the existing Roman and Anglo-Saxon foundations and then explain what Vikings added on top.

A Trading Hub for Northern Europe

Jorvik’s role in international trade networks made it one of the wealthiest towns in early medieval Britain. Norse merchants linked York to Dublin, Bergen, Birka in Sweden and the Russian rivers that ran down to the Black Sea and the Caliphate of Baghdad. Excavations have turned up silk fragments from the eastern Mediterranean, cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean, amber from the Baltic and silver dirhams minted under Abbasid caliphs. The York merchants exported wool, cloth, leather and fine craftwork in return.

By the time of Domesday Book in 1086, York had a population estimated at around 9,000 people — second only to London in England. This was the result of a long process of urban migration that had begun under the Anglo-Saxons and accelerated under the Vikings. Population growth fed economic growth, which in turn pulled in more migrants — a self-reinforcing cycle visible across the period.

It is easy to picture Viking York as a self-contained northern English town. The archaeology tells a different story. Silver dirhams minted in the Abbasid Caliphate of Baghdad were carried up the Russian river system, through the Baltic, and into York merchants’ purses. Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean ended up in Coppergate workshops. Silk fragments from the eastern Mediterranean were stitched into local clothing. Strong answers identify Jorvik as a node in a transcontinental trading network, not just a regional capital — this is what makes the economic factor so striking in the Viking period.

A Mixed Anglo-Scandinavian Culture

By the eleventh century, Viking and Anglo-Saxon residents were difficult to tell apart in everyday life. Historians describe Jorvik’s shared way of life as Anglo-Scandinavian. Norse personal names appear alongside English names in church records; Christian crosses use Norse decorative styles such as the ‘ring chain’ pattern; the city’s archbishops, including Wulfstan II in the early eleventh century, served Norse-descended communities. Religious institutions were not destroyed by Viking arrival — they adapted, and the Church became one of the routes by which Norse migrants were absorbed into wider English society.

Key Fact

The Coppergate excavation (1976–81) revealed Jorvik as a densely populated town of wooden houses, leather and textile workshops, and trade goods from as far as the Indian Ocean and the Caliphate — making the case for Viking York as a major economic and cultural hub, not just a military capital.

lessons.title: Normans, Jews and Medieval Traders, c1066–c1500

before.content_html:
Three Migrant Stories, One Period

Between c1066 and c1500, three very different migrant groups shaped England: the Normans, who arrived as a conquering elite; Jewish communities, brought across by William the Conqueror as royal financiers; and European traders and craftsmen, including the Hanseatic merchants of London’s Steelyard. Reading them side by side teaches the heart of the thematic study — that migration in the same period can be elite, forced, religious or economic all at once. The four key factors (institutions, religion, economic influences, attitudes) all worked differently for each group.

Key Fact

Three medieval migrant groups dominate this period: the Normans (elite military migration after 1066), Jewish communities (brought as financiers, expelled in 1290) and European traders (including Hanseatic merchants at the London Steelyard).

The Normans After 1066

The Norman Conquest of 1066 was a wave of elite migration. William the Conqueror distributed land to perhaps 200 Norman barons, displacing almost the entire Anglo-Saxon landowning class. Domesday Book (1086) records that around 95% of land was held by Norman lords by William’s death. The Norman elite was not, however, a single ethnic group: it included Bretons from western France, Flemings from modern Belgium, and other northern French speakers. Calling them simply ‘the French’ misses how mixed the conquering force actually was.

Norman migration reshaped landownership, the towns, the wool industry and the Church. Romanesque cathedrals replaced Anglo-Saxon ones at Durham, Canterbury and Winchester; the Domesday survey put royal taxation on a new institutional footing; the legal idea of feudal tenure took hold. Norman French became the language of court and law, while ordinary people continued to speak English. Over the centuries the two languages mingled to produce Middle English — one of the deepest impacts of any wave of migration on this island.

Jewish Communities and the Crown

William the Conqueror also brought the first Jewish migrants to England, encouraging them to settle in London and other towns. Jewish communities played a crucial economic role because Christian teaching in this period prohibited Christians from charging interest on loans. Without Jewish moneylenders, the crown could not finance castle-building, military campaigns and royal administration. Aaron of Lincoln (d. 1186) became one of the wealthiest men in England by lending to the crown, the great barons and even Cistercian monasteries.

Jewish migrants in England held the unique legal status of belonging directly to the king. They were taxed through tallage — a special tax that could be raised at royal will, unlike the more limited taxes paid by other subjects. This made Jewish communities both protected and exposed: protected by royal interest, but exposed when popular hostility flared. In 1190, antisemitic violence climaxed in the massacre of Jews at Clifford’s Tower in York. Hundreds of Jewish people died after taking refuge there. The events of 1190 sit alongside Aaron of Lincoln’s wealth as evidence that medieval Jewish life in England mixed royal protection with episodes of devastating violence.

A frequent error is to describe medieval English Jews as freely tolerated until 1290 and then suddenly expelled. The reality was harsher throughout. Heavy royal taxation increased steadily after 1200; the massacres of 1190 (most famously at York) showed how thin royal protection could be; from the 1270s, Edward I tried and failed to make Jewish moneylending profitable for the crown by replacing it with new taxes. The 1290 Edict of Expulsion was the endpoint of a long deterioration, not a sudden reversal of an otherwise tolerant period.

European Traders and the Hanseatic Steelyard

Alongside Norman lords and Jewish financiers, European traders and craftsmen made up the third strand of medieval migration. Many Flemish weavers settled in Norwich, London and the south-east, where the wool industry pulled in skilled labour. The most famous example of European trade migration was the Hanseatic Steelyard in London. Hanseatic merchants ran a fortified trading enclave on the north bank of the Thames, near London Bridge, granted special privileges by Henry III in 1281. From the Steelyard, they imported timber, furs, wax, fish and grain from northern Europe and exported English wool and cloth.

Like Jewish migrants, Hanseatic merchants held a special legal status — the medieval status of alien. Aliens paid higher customs duties, could not own land freely, and lived under their own community rules in defined enclaves. The Steelyard merchants ran a self-governing community with their own warehouses, dining hall and even a small chapel. They prospered until 1598, when Elizabeth I finally revoked their privileges — but for over three centuries they were the most visible foreign-trading community in London.

The Black Death and Migration

The Black Death of 1348–49 killed perhaps a third of the English population and reshaped migration patterns. Survivors moved from villages to towns where labour was suddenly scarce and wages were rising. Skilled craftsmen, especially weavers and dyers, were actively recruited from the Low Countries to fill gaps. The plague did not stop migration — it concentrated it in growing towns and increased demand for European craftspeople. By 1450, around 1.5% of England’s population was made up of recorded aliens, with concentrations in London, Norwich and Southampton.

Comparing the three groups (similarity and difference) is what unlocks higher mark bands. Similarities: all three relied on royal protection and were tied to the institutions key factor; all faced the legal label of ‘alien’ in some form; all faced periods of hostility from the existing population. Differences: Norman lords arrived as a ruling class and replaced English elites; Jewish migrants were brought as economic specialists and ultimately expelled; Hanseatic and Flemish migrants were drawn by trade and cloth wages, accepted but kept legally separate. Strong answers handle these as a comparison rather than three separate stories.

Key Fact

In 1290, Edward I expelled England’s entire Jewish population by royal decree — the first national expulsion of Jews in medieval Europe. England would have no recognised Jewish community again until Cromwell allowed readmission in 1656.

before.content_html:
A New Kind of Migrant Story

Between c1500 and c1700, England changed in ways that reshaped who came and why. The country became a Protestant nation after Henry VIII’s break with Rome (1534), the cloth industry pulled in skilled labour, and global trading companies and privateering tied English ports to Africa, the Americas and Asia. New types of migrant arrived: Protestant religious refugees from Catholic Europe, and small but real numbers of Africans — some free, some unfree — in Tudor and Stuart parishes. The continuity matters too: the legal label of ‘alien’ carried over from medieval England, and most migrants still arrived through the south-east ports.

Key Fact

Three early modern migrant groups dominate this period: Flemish and Walloon Protestant refugees from the 1560s, Huguenots fleeing France after 1685, and Africans — including the trumpeter John Blanke at the Tudor court — documented in parish, court and household records.

Flemish and Walloon Refugees: Sandwich and Canterbury

In the 1560s, Protestant Flemings and Walloons fleeing Spanish Catholic persecution in the Low Countries became the first wave of religious refugees in Protestant England. Elizabeth I and the Privy Council encouraged the arrivals because they brought valuable cloth-making skills the English economy needed. In 1561, Sandwich (Kent) was authorised to take in twenty-five master weavers and their families. Canterbury followed soon after. By the 1580s, Sandwich’s migrant population numbered several thousand — perhaps a third of the town. The arrivals founded their own stranger churches, ran their own poor relief, and used the chancel of St Peter’s in Sandwich for Walloon-language services.

Their economic impact was disproportionate to their numbers. Flemish weavers introduced the ‘new draperies’ — lighter, brighter, more fashionable cloths — which Sandwich and Canterbury exported across northern Europe. They drained marshland for market gardens around Sandwich, growing celery, carrots and cauliflowers on a commercial scale for the first time in England. Local guilds sometimes resented the competition, but corporation records show town authorities defending the strangers’ right to trade because of the customs revenue and tax they generated. The Flemish and Walloon experience set a pattern: religious refugees could be welcomed when their skills met an English economic need.

Huguenots: Spitalfields after 1685

A century later, France produced its own wave of Protestant refugees. In 1685, Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, ending the limited religious tolerance French Protestants had enjoyed since 1598. Around 50,000 Huguenots came to England, the largest single religious migration of the period. Many settled in Spitalfields on the eastern edge of London, where the silk-weaving trade was already established. Charles II encouraged the arrivals through royal proclamations promising denization — a partial legal status that let migrants own property and trade without becoming full subjects. Public collections in parish churches raised funds for the most destitute new arrivals.

In Spitalfields, Huguenot weavers transformed silk production. They built tall houses with broad upper-floor windows to let in the light needed to work the patterned brocades and damasks they specialised in. By 1700, around 25,000 Huguenots lived in Spitalfields and its surrounding parishes. Beyond silk, Huguenot migrants reshaped finance (founding members of the Bank of England in 1694 included Huguenot families), the army (officers serving William III), and clock-making, gunsmithing and jewellery in London’s West End. Within two generations the community had largely assimilated, leaving stranger churches, family names and skilled trades as their lasting mark.

A common error is to describe the Huguenots after 1685 as the first religious refugees in England. The Flemings and Walloons preceded them by more than a century, with Sandwich’s 1561 charter explicitly naming them as religious refugees. The Huguenots were the largest single wave (around 50,000), but they arrived into communities — and a stranger-church model — already shaped by earlier Protestant arrivals from the Low Countries.

Africans in Tudor and Stuart Britain

Far smaller in number, but historically important, was the African presence in Tudor and Stuart Britain. The historian Miranda Kaufmann’s work on parish registers and household accounts has identified more than 360 Africans in England between 1500 and 1640, recorded as servants, court entertainers, divers, sailors and household members. They include John Blanke, a royal trumpeter at the courts of Henry VII and Henry VIII, who appears in payment rolls and the 1511 Westminster Tournament Roll. The presence of these Africans in 1500–1640 dismantles the older idea that Black British history begins with Windrush in 1948.

Other named individuals include Diego, an African mariner who sailed with Francis Drake during the 1577–80 circumnavigation, and Cattelena of Almondsbury, an independent Black woman in Bristol who in 1625 owned her own cow and small property — a rare snapshot of an ordinary working life. Status was uneven: some Africans were enslaved, but courts in this period (notably the 1569 Cartwright case) accepted the principle that England had no laws sanctioning slavery on its own soil. The picture was contradictory — English merchants were beginning to profit from the Atlantic slave trade abroad, while parish registers in England were treating individual Africans as full members of their communities.

A strong answer on this period sets out continuity and change side by side. Continuity: the legal label of ‘alien’ survived from medieval England; the south-east remained the main entry route; economic skills (weaving, finance) drew migrants in. Change: religion now defined who was welcome — Protestant refugees fleeing Catholic regimes were given church charters and royal proclamations, where their medieval predecessors had no such religious framing; Africans appeared in parish registers in numbers larger than was once believed; and, by the 17th century, English involvement in transatlantic slavery added a darker dimension to migration that had no medieval equivalent.

Key Fact

In 1685, Louis XIV’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes triggered the largest single religious migration to England before the 20th century — around 50,000 Huguenots, most settling in Spitalfields and reshaping silk-weaving, finance and skilled trades.

lessons.title: Industrial Britain: Irish, Empire and Refugees, c1700–c1900

before.content_html:
A New Britain, A New Migration

Between c1700 and c1900, Britain became the world’s first industrial nation and the largest empire in history. The factory system, railways, the cotton mills of Lancashire and the docks of Liverpool created a hunger for labour. The Empire stretched from the Caribbean and India to West Africa and the Pacific. Both forces reshaped migration. Famine in Ireland (1845–52) drove the largest wave of European migrants Britain had ever known; the Empire pulled in lascars, ayahs and African mariners; and political upheaval in Europe pushed German socialists, Italian craftsmen and Polish Jews toward Britain’s growing cities. Migration in this period operated through both push and pull factors at scale.

Key Fact

Four migrant streams shaped 18th- and 19th-century Britain: Irish famine migrants from 1845; lascars, ayahs and African seafarers from the Empire; political and economic refugees from Europe (Germans, Italians, Eastern European Jews); and a smaller community of formerly enslaved Africans — including Olaudah Equiano and Mary Prince — whose voices fed the abolitionist cause.

Industrial Pull, European Push

The Industrial Revolution turned northern English towns into factory cities almost overnight. Manchester’s population grew from around 25,000 in 1772 to nearly 250,000 by 1851. Liverpool became the western entrepôt of the Atlantic. Both cities sucked in labour from rural Britain and Ireland. Italian organ-grinders and ice-cream makers settled around Clerkenwell in London, building Britain’s first ‘Little Italy’ by the 1850s. German political refugees fled the failed 1848 revolutions: Karl Marx arrived in London in 1849 and lived in Soho before settling in Kentish Town. German Jewish bankers (the Rothschilds) reshaped London finance from the 1810s. Polish refugees came after the 1863 January Uprising. Each group answered both an industrial pull and a political push.

Smaller groups of migrants reshaped specific trades. German pork butchers were a familiar sight in northern English towns by the 1880s. Italian craftsmen made the mosaics and statues that decorated late-Victorian churches and town halls. Hostility surfaced when economic competition pinched: anti-Italian rioting flared in Manchester in 1894; German bakers were attacked during periodic spy scares from the 1880s. The role of the press matters — the popular press from the 1850s onwards routinely framed migration as a threat to wages, public health or national security, well before the 20th-century debates over the Aliens Act.

Irish Migration: The Largest Wave

The Great Famine of 1845–52, caused by potato blight and worsened by the British government’s reluctance to halt grain exports from Ireland, killed around one million people and forced another million to emigrate. Many travelled the short crossing to Liverpool. By 1851, around 22% of Liverpool’s population was Irish-born. Anti-Irish hostility, much of it shaped by anti-Catholicism, was intense: the slogan ‘No Irish need apply’ appeared in some advertisements in industrial cities, and the press routinely portrayed Irish migrants as carriers of disease in stereotyped cartoons. Yet hostility was patchy. By the 1870s, second-generation Irish migrants were integrating into local trade unions, the Catholic Church and Liberal politics. Working alongside other migrants, they helped shape Britain’s first organised labour movement.

A common error is to assume that because Irish migrants were ‘white’, they faced no prejudice. The opposite is closer to the truth. Anti-Irish hostility ran deep through the mid-19th century, fuelled by anti-Catholic prejudice, fear of cheap labour, and panic about cholera and typhus outbreaks (Liverpool’s 1849 cholera epidemic was widely blamed on Irish migrants). Punch cartoons from the 1860s depicted the Irish in subhuman terms. Newspapers framed Irish neighbourhoods as places of vice and sedition. The Irish are a clear reminder that hostility to migrants in 19th-century Britain was not only racial — religion, class and political fears mattered as much.

Empire and the Atlantic

The Empire produced its own migration streams. Lascars — recruited from Bengal, Yemen and elsewhere — made up roughly a quarter of the British merchant marine by 1855, often working on lower wages than white British sailors. They lodged in dockside lascar boarding houses in London, Liverpool, Cardiff and South Shields. Indian ayahs travelled with British colonial families to care for children, sometimes finding themselves abandoned in London at the end of the voyage; the Ayahs’ Home in Hackney was set up to support stranded women. Smaller numbers of African mariners worked the Atlantic trade routes.

Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade reshaped Black presence in Britain. Enslaved Africans were sometimes brought to Britain by their enslavers, but their legal status was contested. The 1772 Somerset case (in which Lord Mansfield ruled that enslaved persons could not be forcibly removed from England against their will) is often misread as ending slavery in Britain. It did not — it limited removal, and slavery continued legally throughout the British Empire until the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act. Olaudah Equiano’s autobiography (1789) and Mary Prince’s narrative (1831) provided first-person evidence that fuelled the abolitionist cause. Their work shows formerly enslaved Africans as active campaigners for civil liberties, not just as victims of empire.

It is often said that Lord Mansfield’s 1772 Somerset judgement ended slavery in England. The reality is more complex. Mansfield ruled that the enslaved James Somerset could not be forcibly returned to a Caribbean plantation against his will, but he did not declare slavery itself unlawful in England. Adverts for the recapture of runaway enslaved people continued to appear in newspapers into the 1790s, and slavery remained legal across the British Empire until the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act. The Somerset case mattered — it gave abolitionists a legal foothold — but it was a single ambiguous ruling, not the abolition of slavery in Britain.

The Built Environment and Cultural Impact

Migration in this period left a permanent mark on the urban environment. Catholic churches and convents spread across northern industrial cities to serve Irish congregations. The synagogues of Manchester’s Cheetham Hill and London’s East End served growing Jewish populations. Italian cafés, ice-cream parlours and mosaic workshops added a continental layer to British high streets. German political clubs in Soho hosted Marx, Engels and the wider exile community. Migrant labour built much of the railway network, the canals and the docks — many of the navvies who dug the Manchester Ship Canal in the 1880s were Irish. The Empire’s edge thus reached into Britain’s cities, and migration was no longer a south-eastern story alone.

Key Fact

The Great Famine of 1845–52 drove around one million Irish migrants out of Ireland, with Liverpool the main entry point — by 1851, around 22% of Liverpool’s population was Irish-born, the largest single migrant influx Britain had seen.

lessons.title: Case Study: Liverpool and the Irish in the 19th Century

before.content_html:
Why Liverpool?

Liverpool was the indispensable port of 19th-century Atlantic migration. By 1850 it handled around 40% of Britain’s overseas trade. Cotton from American plantations, sugar from the Caribbean, slate from north Wales, and people from Ireland, all moved through the same waterfront. The short sea crossing from Dublin or Cork made Liverpool the cheapest entry point for desperate migrants — a single steerage fare to Liverpool was a fraction of the cost of crossing to New York. Liverpool became Britain’s great entrepôt port: the place where the Empire and Ireland met the British mainland. The 1845–52 Great Famine arrived through its docks.

Key Fact

Liverpool became the main entry point for Irish migration because its location made the crossing cheap (a steerage fare from Dublin was a fraction of the cost to New York), its port was already tied to Atlantic and imperial trade, and its docks needed unskilled labour at exactly the moment a million Irish needed work.

The Famine Wave: Numbers and Timing

During the worst Famine years, 1846–47, perhaps 300,000 Irish migrants landed in Liverpool. Many travelled onward to Manchester, Glasgow or transatlantic ships bound for New York and Boston. But thousands were too poor or too sick to travel further. By 1851, around 22% of Liverpool’s population was Irish-born — the highest concentration in Britain. Whole districts — Vauxhall, Scotland Road, the dockside parishes — became overwhelmingly Irish. The Catholic population of Liverpool grew so fast that the diocese had to build new churches at a pace unmatched anywhere else in industrial Britain.

Most Famine migrants came penniless. The Liverpool Select Vestry recorded over 300,000 Irish receiving poor relief in 1846 alone. The Workhouse Test Order tried to limit relief by requiring migrants to enter the workhouse to qualify, but the system buckled. Father Nugent, a Liverpool-born priest of Irish descent, emerged as the most prominent advocate for the Irish poor in the city, founding refuges, ragged schools and emigration schemes that helped thousands resettle abroad.

Living Conditions: Courts and Cellars

Famine migrants in Liverpool lived in some of the worst housing in Britain. Many were forced into court housing — clusters of small back-to-back houses built around narrow alleys with a shared water pump and a single privy. By 1841 around 38,000 people lived in court housing in Liverpool. Worse still, an estimated 39,000 lived in cellars — basements with little daylight or ventilation. The 1842 Edwin Chadwick Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population had warned that Liverpool was the unhealthiest town in Britain. The arrival of starving Irish migrants made an already overcrowded slum housing system worse, not better.

In 1849 a cholera epidemic killed over 5,000 people in Liverpool. Public-health officials and the press blamed Irish migrants for spreading the disease, even though the cause was contaminated water and inadequate sewers (John Snow’s Soho cholera study, which proved water transmission, came in 1854). The 1849 epidemic burned the connection between Irish migration and disease into popular memory, fuelling hostility for decades. Liverpool became, in the words of one local doctor, ‘the black spot on the Mersey’.

A common error is to assume that the 300,000 Famine migrants who landed in Liverpool stayed there. In reality, the city was a transit point as much as a destination. Many travelled onwards almost immediately — to Manchester for cotton-mill work, to Glasgow for shipbuilding, or to New York and Boston on the transatlantic packets. Liverpool’s 22% Irish-born population by 1851 represents the migrants who could not afford onward fare or were too sick to travel, not the total Irish movement through the port. Strong answers separate ‘Irish in Liverpool’ from ‘Irish through Liverpool’.

Anti-Irish Hostility

Hostility came from many directions. Anti-Catholic prejudice was deeply embedded in mid-Victorian Britain, and Liverpool’s tradition of Orange Order parades made it a flashpoint for sectarian violence between Protestant and Catholic communities. The press routinely portrayed Irish migrants in dehumanising stereotypes — lazy, drunk, criminal. Local employers sometimes posted ‘No Irish Need Apply’ notices, particularly in the 1850s and 1860s. Sectarian rioting flared on St Patrick’s Day, on Orange parade days, and around major political events.

By the 1860s and 1870s, however, the picture was changing. Irish migrants and their British-born children built powerful networks through the Catholic Church, friendly societies and trade unions. By 1900 over 60% of Liverpool dock workers were of Irish descent. Catholic schools served the children of migrants, and the city sent two Irish Nationalist MPs to Westminster between 1885 and 1929. Hostility persisted but coexisted with growing Irish political and economic power.

Liverpool’s Irish-descended population stayed visibly Irish into the 20th century — in a way that, for example, the German pork-butcher community of Manchester did not. Several factors compounded. Liverpool had ongoing migration from Ireland into the early 1900s, refreshing the community. The Catholic Church operated as an active institution — not just a place of worship but a network of schools, hospitals, social clubs and emigrant aid. Sectarian violence with the Orange Order kept group identity politically charged. And the dock economy generated tightly clustered Irish working communities along the waterfront. Identity was reproduced, not just inherited.

Long-Term Impact on Liverpool

By 1900 Liverpool was fundamentally an Irish-influenced city. The Catholic cathedral was started (though not completed until much later); Irish-descended families dominated whole trades; Irish accents shaded into the new ‘Scouse’ identity that would define the 20th-century city. Anti-Irish hostility had not vanished, but the migrants of 1845–52 had become builders of one of Britain’s most distinctive urban cultures. Liverpool became, alongside the East End for Jewish migrants and Spitalfields for Huguenots, a case study in how migration reshapes a single place across decades of change.

Key Fact

The 1849 cholera epidemic killed over 5,000 people in Liverpool, and the press blamed Irish migrants for spreading disease — even though John Snow’s 1854 study would later prove cholera was waterborne. The epidemic burned the link between Irish migration and disease into Victorian public opinion.

Use precise period vocabulary — entrepôt, Select Vestry, court housing, Orange Order, Scouse — for SPaG marks where the question awards them.

lessons.title: Case Study: Jewish East End and the Aliens Act, c1880–1914

before.content_html:
Why the East End?

Between 1881 and 1914, around 150,000 Eastern European Jewish migrants settled in Britain, the great majority in the East End of London. They arrived fleeing waves of pogroms — organised violent attacks on Jewish communities in the Russian Empire that began after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in March 1881. New Russian laws (the ‘May Laws’ of 1882) restricted where Jews could live, study and trade. The East End offered three things at once: cheap lodging in Whitechapel, Spitalfields and Stepney; a thriving garment trade that needed cheap labour; and an existing small Anglo-Jewish community whose synagogues and welfare societies could absorb new arrivals. Migration in this period was driven by religious push and economic pull working together.

Key Fact

Around 150,000 Eastern European Jewish migrants came to Britain between 1881 and 1914, settling overwhelmingly in the East End. They were driven by Russian pogroms (push), pulled by the East End garment trade (economic), and supported by an existing Anglo-Jewish community whose synagogues and welfare societies absorbed the arrivals.

Sweatshops and the Garment Trade

Most migrants entered the sweated trades — tailoring, cap-making, boot- and shoe-making, cabinet-making — that flourished in the East End. By 1900 around 60% of London tailoring was done in the East End, much of it by Jewish migrants. The work was piece-rate, performed in small workshops in tenement back rooms, where men, women and children worked 12-hour days for very low wages. Trade unions including the Hebrew Cabinet Makers’ Association and the Jewish Tailors’ Union organised through the 1880s and 1890s, demanding limits on hours and minimum rates. The 1889 London Dock Strike and the wider East End labour movement drew Jewish workers into mainstream British trade unionism.

Beyond the workshops, Jewish migrants reshaped the East End’s street life. Yiddish theatres opened in Whitechapel; the Yiddish press ran multiple daily papers including the Yidisher Ekspres; kosher butchers, bakers and synagogues filled streets that had been Huguenot two centuries earlier (the Brick Lane synagogue had begun life as a Huguenot chapel before becoming a Methodist chapel and then, from 1898, the Spitalfields Great Synagogue). Mutual-aid societies, hevra (small synagogues), and the Jewish Board of Guardians provided welfare. The community also produced a generation of socialist and trade-union activists, including the journalist Morris Winchevsky, who became central voices in early British labour politics.

The Role of the Media

From the 1880s, sections of the British press treated Jewish migration as a national problem. Newspapers like the Daily Mail (founded 1896) and the older Daily News ran scare stories about ‘destitute aliens’ flooding the East End and undermining native wages. Cartoons depicted Jewish migrants in stereotyped, often antisemitic terms. A Royal Commission on Alien Immigration (1902–03) investigated, hearing evidence from Jewish community leaders, social workers and trade unionists alongside hostile politicians. The press response was often more inflammatory than the Commission’s findings. The role of the popular press in shaping public attitudes — well before radio or television — was a defining feature of late-Victorian and Edwardian migration debates.

A common assumption is that hostile tabloid coverage of migrants began in the late 20th century. The pattern is much older. The 1880s and 1890s saw the British press routinely framing Eastern European Jewish migrants as a public-health and economic threat. Headlines about ‘the alien invasion’ appeared two decades before the Aliens Act. The new mass-circulation press (the Daily Mail from 1896) accelerated the pattern, but the template was set earlier. Strong answers identify the press as a third factor (alongside push and pull) shaping the Jewish migrant experience.

The Aliens Act 1905

In 1902 the British Brothers’ League was founded by Major William Evans-Gordon, the Conservative MP for Stepney. Its rallies in the East End demanded an end to Jewish immigration. The campaign succeeded: the Conservative government’s Aliens Act 1905 — Britain’s first peacetime immigration control — gave immigration officers power to refuse entry to migrants who could not support themselves, who were judged to be of bad character, or who had a criminal record. It exempted political refugees in principle, and wealthy migrants who could pay their passage in cabin class were not subject to inspection at all. The Act was administered by the new Aliens Inspectorate at the major ports.

The 1905 Act did not stop Jewish migration outright. Numbers continued to rise until the First World War, partly because the Liberal government from 1906 administered the Act loosely — Home Secretary Herbert Gladstone instructed inspectors to give migrants the benefit of the doubt. But the Act marked a clear break from the 19th-century tradition of free entry. It established the principle that Britain could close its doors at will. Later acts — the 1914 Aliens Restriction Act, the 1919 Aliens Restriction Act, the 1962 and 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Acts — built on the 1905 framework.

A frequent error is to describe the 1905 Aliens Act as a general cap on foreign immigration. It was nothing of the kind. The Act’s exemptions for wealthy migrants and (in principle) political refugees made clear that the target was poor Jewish migrants from Eastern Europe specifically. Migrants travelling cabin class were not even inspected. The British Brothers’ League’s rallies in Stepney made the antisemitic intent visible at the time. Strong answers identify the Act as the first piece of British immigration law shaped explicitly by hostility to one specific group.

Impact and Legacy

By 1914 the East End had been remade by Jewish migration. Synagogues, Yiddish theatres, kosher food shops, and trade-union halls clustered along Whitechapel Road, Brick Lane and Commercial Street. The community produced doctors, lawyers, writers and politicians within a generation. Mutual-aid networks (the Jewish Board of Guardians, hevra synagogues, friendly societies) modelled welfare provision that fed into wider British social policy. At the same time, the 1905 Aliens Act and the press hostility that produced it set a template for 20th-century immigration politics. Both legacies — the cultural transformation of east London and the legal-political restriction of free entry — can be traced back to the same three decades.

Key Fact

The 1905 Aliens Act was Britain’s first peacetime immigration control. It targeted poor Eastern European Jewish migrants specifically, exempted wealthy migrants entirely, and established the principle — new to Britain — that the state could refuse entry to migrants at will.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Around 150,000 Eastern European Jewish migrants came to Britain 1881–1914, fleeing pogroms in the Russian Empire and pulled by the East End sweated trades; by 1900 around 60% of London tailoring was done in the East End.
  • The popular press from the 1880s framed Jewish migration as a threat — the Daily Mail from 1896 amplified the message — and the British Brothers’ League (1901), founded by Major William Evans-Gordon, lobbied parliament for restrictions.
  • The 1905 Aliens Act was Britain’s first peacetime immigration control. It exempted wealthy migrants and targeted poor Jewish refugees specifically, establishing the legal principle that the state could refuse entry — a foundation for all later 20th-century immigration legislation.

Indicative content — arguments supporting the role of the media as most important: • Newspapers (the Daily Mail from 1896, the Daily News, popular illustrated weeklies) framed Jewish migration as an alien invasion through the 1880s and 1890s. • Press coverage of the 1902–03 Royal Commission on Alien Immigration amplified hostile testimony and created sustained public pressure. • Mass-circulation tabloids reached new audiences and politicised migration as never before. Indicative content — arguments against (other factors mattered as much or more): • The British Brothers’ League (1901), founded by Major William Evans-Gordon, MP for Stepney, organised East End rallies that gave anti-immigration politics a parliamentary champion. • Economic competition in the East End sweated trades fuelled fears that cheap Jewish labour would undercut native wages. • The Conservative government under Arthur Balfour saw electoral advantage in restricting immigration; the Act was a political response, not just a media response. • The role of religion: antisemitic prejudice predated the press scare and shaped how stories about Jewish migrants were received. • The cumulative pressure of 150,000 arrivals over two decades created a felt sense of urgency in the East End that none of the individual factors fully captures alone. Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the role of the media against at least one other factor (the British Brothers’ League, economic competition, government policy), uses accurate Edwardian vocabulary, includes a self-generated factor alongside the stimulus, and reaches a clear judgement. Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended. Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1905 Aliens Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• It was Britain’s first peacetime immigration control law.
• It gave immigration officers power to refuse entry to migrants who could not support themselves, who were judged to be of bad character, or who had a criminal record.
• It exempted political refugees in principle.
• It exempted wealthy migrants travelling in cabin class from inspection altogether, focusing the Act on poor migrants in steerage.
• It was administered by the new Aliens Inspectorate at the major ports.
• It was passed by the Conservative government under Prime Minister Arthur Balfour in 1905; the Liberal government from 1906 administered it loosely.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to immigration controls without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the East End of London became the focus of Jewish migration in this period.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• An existing Anglo-Jewish community provided synagogues, the Jewish Board of Guardians and welfare societies that could absorb new arrivals.
• The East End’s sweated trades (tailoring, cap-making, boot-making) offered immediate piece-rate work without English-language skills.
• Cheap tenement housing in Whitechapel, Spitalfields and Stepney made the area accessible to destitute migrants.
• Yiddish-language institutions (newspapers, theatres, religious schools) flourished, reinforcing the area’s status as a Jewish neighbourhood.
• Trade-union organisation (Hebrew Cabinet Makers’ Association, Jewish Tailors’ Union) gave migrant workers a stake in the wider labour movement.
• Many migrants intended to move on to America; the East End was the cheapest stopping point in Britain, and many ended up settling there.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific detail (named institutions, specific places, dated developments) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the East End without explaining the focus.

lessons.title: Modern Britain: Wars, Empire's End and the Law, c1900–present

before.content_html:
A New Century, A New Politics of Migration

Between c1900 and the present, migration to Britain was reshaped by world wars, the end of the Empire, and a new framework of immigration law. The 1905 Aliens Act had already established that the state could refuse entry; the 20th century saw that principle extended to almost every group in turn. At the same time, two world wars brought European refugees and colonial troops; decolonisation drew Caribbean and South Asian migrants from the wider Commonwealth; and EU enlargement in 2004 delivered the largest single peacetime arrival in British history. Push and pull factors remained the same shape, but the politics around them changed completely.

Key Fact

Four major migrant streams shaped modern Britain: World War refugees (Belgians 1914, European Jews 1933–39, Poles after 1945); Commonwealth migrants from the Caribbean (Windrush 1948), South Asia and East Africa (Ugandan Asians 1972); EU migrants after 2004 (around one million Poles by 2017); and asylum seekers throughout. Each was shaped by a specific piece of legislation.

Wars and Refugees

The two world wars produced the largest refugee movements of the century. In autumn 1914, around 250,000 Belgian refugees fled the German invasion and arrived in Britain — the largest single refugee influx Britain had then experienced. They were initially welcomed as victims of the ‘Hun’ and dispersed across more than 2,500 War Refugees Committee local groups. Most returned home after 1918. The First World War also brought lascars, Caribbean and African colonial troops to British ports, and a small Chinese seafaring community to Limehouse. From 1933 around 70,000 European Jews escaped Nazi persecution to Britain, including the 10,000 Jewish children of the 1938–39 Kindertransport. Polish service personnel who had fought with the Allies were given the right to settle by the 1947 Polish Resettlement Act — the first major piece of British legislation explicitly designed to welcome a refugee group.

War also reshaped the institutions handling migration. The 1914 Aliens Restriction Act — passed within days of the outbreak of war — gave the Home Office sweeping powers over ‘enemy aliens’. The 1919 Aliens Restriction (Amendment) Act extended these wartime controls into peacetime. By the late 1930s, refugees from Nazism faced visa requirements that had not existed in 1905. The arc from 1905 to 1939 shows the state acquiring more and more discretion over who could enter Britain.

Empire’s End and the 1948 Nationality Act

The post-war story is dominated by decolonisation and the British Nationality Act of 1948. The Act created a single status of ‘Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies’ that gave everyone in Britain and its colonies the right to live and work in Britain. Its primary purpose was to keep a common citizenship across the Dominions (Canada, Australia, New Zealand) at a moment when those countries were drafting their own nationality laws. Caribbean migration was an unintended consequence. On 22 June 1948, the Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 mainly Jamaican passengers, many of them ex-RAF servicemen returning to a Britain short of labour. Smaller Caribbean ships had arrived earlier, but the press coverage of the Windrush made it the symbol of a new era.

Caribbean migration grew steadily through the 1950s, encouraged by London Transport, the new National Health Service (founded 1948) and British Rail, which actively recruited workers from Barbados, Jamaica and Trinidad. Migration from India, Pakistan and (after 1971) Bangladesh followed; East African Asians arrived after Kenya’s independence and the 1972 Ugandan expulsion. The 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Act and 1971 Immigration Act narrowed Commonwealth migration sharply. By the 1970s the post-war ‘open door’ was effectively closed.

A common error is to claim that the 1948 Act was designed to invite Caribbean labour to Britain. The opposite is closer to the truth. The Act’s primary purpose was to preserve a common Imperial citizenship after the white Dominions began drafting their own nationality laws. Civil servants and ministers were genuinely surprised when Caribbean men — who held the same citizenship in law — began arriving in numbers from 1948. By 1962 the same governing party, now anxious about scale, would pass the Commonwealth Immigrants Act to limit the migration the 1948 Act had accidentally enabled. Strong answers identify the 1948 Act as a Dominions law that produced an unintended Caribbean migration.

The Empire Windrush’s arrival on 22 June 1948 is the iconic image of post-war Caribbean migration, but it was not the first ship. The Ormonde had brought around 100 Jamaicans in March 1947 and the Almanzora followed at the end of that year. Caribbean servicemen had also been stationed in Britain through the war. Windrush matters because the Pathé newsreel of its arrival made the migration visible to the British public, but it was not unique. Strong answers describe Windrush as iconic rather than as a first.

The Restriction Era: 1962 to 1981

The Conservative government’s Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 ended free movement from the Commonwealth. Migrants from former colonies now needed a Ministry of Labour voucher to enter Britain, allocated by job category. Numbers fell sharply after 1962 but family reunion continued. A second Commonwealth Immigrants Act in 1968 was passed in just three days specifically to keep East African Asians with British passports out of Britain — many had fled Kenya’s ‘Africanisation’ policies. Enoch Powell’s ‘Rivers of Blood’ speech of 20 April 1968 sat alongside this legislation, framing Commonwealth migration as a threat. The 1971 Immigration Act narrowed entry further to those with a parent or grandparent born in Britain (‘patriality’), a measure that effectively privileged the descendants of white Dominions settlers. The 1981 British Nationality Act completed the framework by abolishing the ‘Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies’ status created in 1948.

Anti-discrimination law developed in parallel. The 1965 Race Relations Act made discrimination unlawful in public places; the 1968 Race Relations Act extended it to housing and employment; the 1976 Race Relations Act created the Commission for Racial Equality. The 1972 Ugandan Asian expulsion brought around 28,000 East African Asian refugees to Britain — many of them to Leicester — and prompted both the toughening of immigration law and the strengthening of race-relations law in the same decade.

EU Enlargement and the Modern Era

In 2004, eight new EU member states (the ‘A8’), including Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and the Baltic states, gained free movement rights. Britain (alongside Ireland and Sweden) opened its labour market immediately rather than imposing the seven-year transitional controls used by France and Germany. The result was the largest single peacetime migration in British history: around one million Polish migrants by 2017 (around 900,000 still resident). The 2016 Brexit referendum was driven, in part, by the politics of this migration, and the 2021 EU Settlement Scheme brought an end to free movement. The roles of the popular press, of national newspapers and of social media in shaping public attitudes through this period mirror, on a much larger scale, the press hostility to Eastern European Jewish migrants in the 1880s and 1890s. The 2018 Windrush scandal — in which long-settled Caribbean migrants were wrongly threatened with deportation — revealed the human consequences of layered immigration laws stretching back to the 1962 Act.

Key Fact

Four pieces of legislation shaped post-war migration: the 1948 British Nationality Act (open Commonwealth citizenship); the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act (vouchers required); the 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Act (East African Asians); and the 1971 Immigration Act (‘patriality’). Each was a response to the migration the previous one had produced.
before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain Why’ on post-war migration, sequence two genuinely different reasons drawn from the spec’s key factors: institutions (legislation — the 1948 British Nationality Act, the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act); and economic influences (post-war labour shortage, NHS and London Transport recruitment from the Caribbean). Name dated events (Windrush 22 June 1948; A8 enlargement 2004) and named groups (Belgians 1914, Kindertransport 1938–39, Ugandan Asians 1972, Polish A8 migrants). For 16-mark judgement essays with SPaG, use precise period vocabulary (decolonisation, Commonwealth, patriality, asylum, free movement) and treat legislation as a chain of cause and consequence — the 1962 Act responded to Caribbean migration; the 1968 Act responded to East African Asians; the 1971 Act responded to both.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Caribbean migration to Britain in the years after 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two valid features):
• It was made possible by the 1948 British Nationality Act, which gave Citizens of the UK and Colonies the right to live and work in Britain.
• The arrival of the Empire Windrush at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with 492 mainly Jamaican passengers became its iconic moment.
• Public bodies such as London Transport, British Rail and the new NHS (founded 1948) actively recruited workers from Barbados, Jamaica and Trinidad.
• Earlier ships such as the Ormonde (March 1947) had already brought Caribbean migrants — Windrush was iconic, not unique.
• Many early arrivals were ex-RAF servicemen returning to a Britain short of post-war labour.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support (named ships, dates, employers).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to Caribbean migration without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the British Nationality Act of 1948 led to large-scale Caribbean migration to Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Institutions: the 1948 Act created a single ‘Citizen of the UK and Colonies’ status that gave Caribbean people the legal right to live and work in Britain. The Act’s primary purpose was to preserve a common citizenship across the white Dominions; Caribbean migration was an unintended consequence.
• Economic influences: post-war Britain faced a severe labour shortage as cities rebuilt after the Blitz and the new welfare state expanded. The NHS (founded 1948), London Transport and British Rail actively recruited workers from Barbados, Jamaica and Trinidad.
• Connection to the Empire: many Caribbean men had served in the RAF and merchant marine during the Second World War and saw Britain as the ‘mother country’.
• The arrival of the Empire Windrush on 22 June 1948, widely covered in newsreels, made the legal right visible and encouraged later arrivals.
• Limited opportunity in the Caribbean: high unemployment in Jamaica and the closing of the United States as a destination after 1952 immigration restrictions made Britain the obvious choice.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific detail (the 1948 Act, named employers, named events) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of post-war Britain without explaining the reasons.

• In autumn 1914 around 250,000 Belgian refugees had arrived in Britain fleeing the German invasion — the largest single refugee influx until then.
• The 1947 Polish Resettlement Act gave Polish service personnel and their families the right to settle in Britain — the first British law designed to welcome a refugee group.
• Many Polish, Italian, Ukrainian and Latvian European Volunteer Workers were recruited from displaced-persons camps to fill labour shortages between 1946 and 1949.
• The 1914 Aliens Restriction Act and 1919 Aliens Restriction (Amendment) Act extended Home Office discretion over ‘enemy aliens’ into peacetime.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail (numbers, dates, named groups).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to wartime migration without identifying a feature.
